profile.name: Eurythmy
profile.tagline: An esoteric art of movement making visible the sounds of speech and music.
profile.insight: Eurythmy treats vowels and consonants as physical air-gestures, making the spoken word and musical melody literally visible through human movement.
profile.profile: Eurythmy is an expressive movement art created in the early 20th century by Rudolf Steiner and Marie Steiner-von Sivers. It translates the sounds of speech and the tones of music into visible, disciplined gestures of the arms and body. Rooted in anthroposophy, it is performed as an artistic stage discipline, taught in Waldorf schools, and applied in anthroposophic medicine.
profile.profile_long:
Eurythmy is a disciplined art of movement conceived in 1911 by Rudolf Steiner in conjunction with his wife, Marie Steiner-von Sivers. The practice emerged when a young girl named Lory Smits sought a career in movement, prompting Steiner to suggest exploring human anatomy, Greek sculpture, and the movement implicit in spoken language. Developed further through the Anthroposophical Society's dramas at the Goetheanum in Dornach, Switzerland, the art form expanded into public touring by 1919. Steiner viewed eurythmy as an external proof of humanity's connection to the supersensible world.

In performance, eurythmy is divided primarily into tone eurythmy and speech eurythmy. When performed to music, the three major elements of melody, harmony, and rhythm are expressed through the rise and fall of pitches, the tension and release of consonances and dissonances, and spatial dynamics. Speech eurythmy translates the audible sounds of vowels and consonants—such as the open position of an 'A' or the sharp plosive nature of a 'K'—into visible air-gestures. The performer's body avoids pantomime or mimicry, acting instead as the direct visible equivalent of the spoken word or musical phrase.

Costumes typically consist of long, loose fabrics in characteristic colors that accentuate movement rather than bodily form, accompanied by stage lighting that saturates the space. Pedagogically, eurythmy has been a core component of Waldorf school curricula since 1919. Exercises begin with straight lines and curves, advancing to complex geometric patterns like the Harmonious Eight and the Curve of Cassini, often utilizing copper rods and balls to build balance and spatial awareness. Additionally, eurythmy is integrated into anthroposophic medicine as a therapeutic practice, though it remains unrecognised by mainstream medical science.

sections.origins_and_history: Conceived in 1911 and 1912 by Rudolf Steiner and Marie Steiner-von Sivers, eurythmy began when young Lory Smits sought a movement career. It was integrated into anthroposophical dramas at the Goetheanum in Dornach, Switzerland, with the first ensemble touring in Switzerland, the Netherlands, and Germany in 1919.
sections.how_it_is_danced: A disciplined art of movement of the arms and body expressing speech vowels and consonants, musical melody, and harmony. Dancers cultivate straight lines, curves, spatial directions, and geometric floor figures.
sections.music_and_instruments: Tone eurythmy expresses melody (rise, fall, pitch, intervals), harmony (tension, release, dissonance, consonance, major/minor moods), and rhythm (slow for long notes, quick for short notes). Individual instruments' timbres are expressed by specific eurythmists.
sections.costume_and_setting: Long, loose fabrics of characteristic colors that accentuate movements rather than bodily form. Lighting saturates the space and shifts with the moods of the performance.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed as a stage art, integrated into Waldorf school curricula for pedagogical development, and used within anthroposophic medicine for therapeutic purposes. Steiner viewed it as an expression of the supersensible world.

profile.sacred_note: Associated with anthroposophy and the supersensible world, viewed by its founder as a direct external proof of a human's share in the supersensible world.

teaching.rhythm: Follows the meter, tempo, and notes of musical melody or speech sounds
teaching.formation: Geometric figures, straight lines, curves, Harmonious Eight, Curve of Cassini
teaching.level_notes: Begins with straight lines and curves, proceeding to more complicated geometric figures and choreographed forms.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Livelier and more contoured movements for quick notes, slower, dreamier movements for longer notes
music_profile.vocal_style: spoken texts such as poetry, stories, or plays; audible sounds of speech
music_profile.sound_description: Tone eurythmy expresses melody rise and fall, pitch, and intervals, while harmony moves between tension and release, matching classical chamber or symphonic compositions.

movement_profile.posture: Disciplined posture cultivating a feeling for straight lines and curves, spatial directions, contraction and expansion
movement_profile.footwork: Human step, spatial walking along geometric paths
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Disciplined movement of the arms and body expressing vowels and consonants
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Movements in space forward, backward, up, down, left, right; geometric patterns like Harmonious Eight and Curve of Cassini
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Livelier movements for quick notes, slower for longer tones

signature_moves.description: Dynamic movement sequence forming a figure-eight pattern

signature_moves.name: Curve of Cassini
signature_moves.description: Metamorphosing geometric pattern used in pedagogical exercises

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Moves into active front space and passive back space; up and down spatial directions
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: It is not meant to be pantomime or mimic, nor illustrative or interpretive gesture.
